en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 58.
The Training Rule on Making Oneself Ugly.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus and wanderers were traveling on the road from Sāketa to Sāvatthī. Robbers came out on the way and robbed them.
The king’s officers from Sāvatthī came out, seized those robbers together with their goods, and sent a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying:
"Come, venerable sirs; recognize and take each your own robe."
The bhikkhus did not recognize [the robes].
They complained, grumbled, and protested:
"How can it be that the venerable ones do not recognize their own respective robes?"
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled; having given a Dhamma talk to the monks that was appropriate and suitable for them, he addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, I will lay down a training rule for the monks based on ten reasons:
for the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha … [and so on] … for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"When a monk receives a new robe, he must apply one of the three kinds of disfigurement:
either blue, mud-color, or dark brown. If a monk does not apply one of the three kinds of disfigurement—"
If one should use a new robe that makes it discolored, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"New" means that which has not yet been made allowable.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes.
"One of the three ways of making discolored" means that one of the three methods for discoloring [the robe] should be adopted.
At the very least, it should be taken up even with the tip of a blade of kusa grass.
"Blue" refers to two kinds of blue: the blue of bell-metal and the blue of the palāsa tree.
"Mud" is said to be water.
"Blackish-brown" means...
Whatever is blackish-blue:
if a monk, without taking up any one of the three methods for disfiguring [the cloth],

even if only as much as the tip of a blade of kusa grass, uses a new robe without having taken up any one of the three methods for disfiguring it, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
If one consumes what has not been given while perceiving it as not given, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one consumes what has not been given while being in doubt, there is an offense of expiation.
If one consumes what has not been given while perceiving it as given, there is an offense of expiation.
If it has been taken and he perceives it as not taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it has been taken and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it has been taken and he perceives it as taken, there is no offense.
There is no offense if,
having taken it, one consumes it,
or if the allowable time has expired.
The border that has been made allowable becomes worn out;
what was not made allowable is sewn together with what has been made allowable at the edge.
In the windward direction, in the vicinity,
for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
the eighth training rule concerning making [the robes] ugly is finished.
